newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian minister decries non-ferrous scrap exports.
newsitem.headline: Russian minister decries non-ferrous scrap exports.

text.p: Russian criminal groups exporting non-ferrous scrap metals are harming the economy, Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Davydov, who is in charge of foreign trade, said on Monday.
Davydov, quoted by Interfax news agency, repeated statements made by other officials in 1996 that Moscow would probably use quotas or licenses to regulate the scrap metals trade.

"The problem of unlimited, non-ferrous scrap exports has such a direct relationship to the personal security of Russians, whose life is exposed to a genuine threat as a result of the actions of robbers of ready-made products produced from non-ferrous metals," he said.

"In the pursuit of easy gains against the backdrop of higher demand abroad for non-ferrous metals, criminal groups are removing metal details, parts and entire units from transport and mechanical structures and exporting them as scrap metal."
Davydov did not mention specific metals.
But he said the time had come to introduce licenc es or quotas to solve the problem and that the government had discussed the matter.

"Increasing to a maximum level the processing of non-ferrous scrap will lead to a more rational use of natural resources and will help us support strategic reserves at a level sufficient for national security," he said.

The Industry Ministry's bid for quotas limiting all scrap metals exports to two million tonnes a year to provide feedstocks for domestic metallurgical enterprises was rejected by government commission in September 1996 in favour of a licensing scheme.
About 30 percent of Russian copper is produced from scrap metal.
